subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: Hafsa, when I was small we were three children in the house, and every evening the same fight: who laid the table, who swept, who watered the plants. So one Sunday I, Tenzin, took a big sheet of paper. We wrote the chores across the top and our three names down the side, then drew arrows so the names moved one place each week. Pinned on the kitchen door, everyone could see whose turn it was. I liked it because nobody had to say 'You always do less'. The fight faded, though my brother still forgot the plants now and then, and we laughed at that.

qa.q: Where was the chore chart pinned?
qa.a: The chart was pinned on the kitchen door.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the chart in the kitchen?
qa.a: Tenzin liked it because nobody had to argue about who did less, which suggests a feeling of relief and fairness.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped end the fights, and why?
qa.a: Making the names move one place each week helped, because everyone did every chore and the turns were visible.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's brother have seen the chart?
qa.a: Tenzin's brother sometimes forgot the plants, and the group laughed about it, so the chart probably felt fair even when a turn was missed.

grounding: Three siblings write chores on a chart with rotating names so the sharing is open and nobody feels they do more than others.

subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: When Mummy's leg went into plaster, the flat fell apart in two days. Plates piled up, the tulsi drooped, and Jyoti, Urmila and their little brother Raju were fighting about who did what. 'I watered the plants yesterday!' 'I laid the table twice!' Jyoti took a chart paper and drew three columns: laying the table, watering the plants, sweeping. Down the side, Monday to Sunday. Then she wrote their names across, shifting one box each day, so the jobs rotated. She stuck it on the fridge. Mummy read it from the sofa and laughed. On Thursday, when Raju groaned about sweeping, Urmila just tapped the chart. Raju picked up the broom.

qa.q: How did Raju seem to feel about sweeping on Thursday?
qa.a: He groaned, so he felt reluctant, but he accepted it when Urmila tapped the chart.

qa.q: Why did rotating the names help stop the fights?
qa.a: Everyone could see the turns change each day, so nobody could claim to be doing more than the others.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the chart?
qa.a: Mummy reads it from the sofa and laughs, so she seems relieved and amused that the children sorted it out themselves.

grounding: Shows three siblings making a chore chart with rotating names for laying the table, watering plants and sweeping, so nobody feels they do more.

subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: In their Dehradun flat, every evening ended the same way: 'Why do I always lay the table?' 'You never water the plants!' Chetan, the eldest of the three, finally got out a sheet of chart paper and sat his sisters Nidhi and Gauri at the table. They listed the jobs: lay the table, water the balcony plants, sweep the hall. Then Chetan drew a grid for the week and wrote their names in turns, moving along one each day. 'Monday I lay, Nidhi waters, Gauri sweeps. Tuesday, we shift.' Gauri checked it twice to make sure it was fair. Their neighbour Tenzin, visiting on Saturday, saw it on the fridge and asked if he could copy it for his house.

qa.q: Which city is their flat in?
Why did Gauri check the chart twice?
qa.a: She wanted to be sure it was fair, probably worried she'd been doing more than her share.

qa.q: What else could make the chart work well?
qa.a: A swap rule for busy days, agreed by all three; open, rotating turns are what stop anyone feeling they do more.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see the chart?
qa.a: Tenzin likes it enough to ask if he can copy it for his own house.

grounding: Illustrates three siblings writing chores on a chart with names rotating each day, so the turns are open and nobody feels they do more.
